We propose PhysGuard, a physics-preserving framework for accurate sim-to-real adaptation of neural operators. Specifically, PhysGuard uses the empirical Fisher Information Matrix computed on simulation data to identify physics-critical parameter directions, then restricts fine-tuning updates to directions that do not interfere with them. A layer-wise Gram-matrix formulation makes this efficient for models with millions of parameters, while an adaptive threshold automatically determines the protected subspace size. A spectral probe experiment shows that the dominant Fisher directions are strongly associated with low-frequency output structures. Experiments on benchmark across four neural operator architectures and different physical systems show that PhysGuard performs strongly on most evaluation metrics compared to baselines. The benefits are most evident under severe domain shift, where it reduces low-frequency error by up to 32% compared to standard fine-tuning while maintaining adaptability. Our code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Jung-Hoon Cho,Heling Zhang,Siqi Du,Roy Dong,Cathy Wu
title: Formalizing and Estimating Task-Space Complexity for Zero-shot Generalization
abstract: Generalization is crucial for modern control, but learning across tasks can be costly. Recent work shows that zero-shot transfer, in which a controller designed for a source task is directly deployed to a target task, can achieve strong performance. We formalize task-space complexity, which characterizes the difficulty of achieving sufficiently good performance across a collection of tasks, by casting source selection as a covering problem. We provide bounds on the complexity and demonstrate its applicability.

authors: Zhengpeng Xie,Li Lyna Zhang,Zeke Xie,Mao Yang
title: Trust Region Policy Distillation
abstract: Big goals are hard to achieve all at once; breaking them into small steps is wiser. We present Trust Region Policy Distillation (TOP-D), which transforms the notoriously unstable, high-variance On-Policy Distillation (OPD) into a stable training paradigm by dynamically constructing a proximal teacher. Theoretically, we establish a rigorous framework demonstrating that TOP-D inherently controls gradient variance. By providing a formal global convergence analysis alongside a monotonic improvement bound, we mathematically formalize the reliability and stability of the overall training dynamics. Empirically, TOP-D dramatically enhances training stability, sample efficiency, and final performance on mathematical reasoning tasks. More importantly, TOP-D introduces zero additional computational overhead, positioning itself as a promising alternative to the well-established OPD paradigm.

authors: Ziqi Yin,Jianyang Gao,Peiqi Yin,Jiangneng Li,Gao Cong
title: LiteTopK: Exploiting the Curse of Dimensionality for a Fused Indexer-TopK Kernel in Long-Context Sparse Attention
abstract: Indexer-TopK, which computes scores and selects the top-$k$ candidates, is a key primitive in long-context sparse attention for large language models and vector retrieval for recommendation systems and vector databases. However, existing GPU-based Indexer-TopK kernels like DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) typically separate scoring from selection and materialize the full score matrix in high-bandwidth memory. This strategy is inefficient for large score matrices, such as those encountered in long-context sparse attention, due to excessive global-memory traffic, costly synchronization, and prohibitive memory overhead. In this study, motivated by the curse of dimensionality, we observe that sparse attention scores exhibit a concentration phenomenon, with scores falling within a narrow range. Based on this observation, we propose LiteTopK, an efficient fused Indexer-TopK kernel. LiteTopK samples a small subset of data to estimate query-data score ranges, then partitions candidates into bins accordingly. This design allows LiteTopK to maintain a slightly relaxed threshold online and write back only promising candidates, reducing unnecessary I/O and memory overhead while preserving exact top-$k$ correctness. Building on LiteTopK, we further propose LiteDSA, which packs the overlapping candidates of neighboring query tokens into a shared key/value list for joint attention and uses per-query masks to preserve each token's original top-$k$ membership while reducing memory traffic. We integrate LiteTopK into three widely used LLM training and inference systems: vLLM, SGLang, and Megatron-LM. Experiments in a production environment with eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs demonstrate prefill speedups of up to $1.49\times$ across GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Hy-4-Preview at a context length of 1M tokens, without compromising model capabilities.

authors: Binglin Wu,Chuan Yue,Yingyi Zhang,Xianneng Li,Ruyue Deng,Weiru Zhang,Xiaoyi Zeng
title: Beyond Single-Episode Optimization: Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding for Long-Term Advertising Effectiveness
abstract: Auto-bidding systems optimize bids to maximize value under efficiency constraints such as Cost-Per-Action (CPA). Existing methods treat each day as an independent episode. However, many advertisers produce value so sparsely that per-day efficiency ratios become statistically unreliable, undermining advertiser retention. Platforms therefore evaluate window-level efficiency over sliding windows of $W{=}7$ days, ensuring fair evaluation and long-term advertising effectiveness. This creates cross-episode coupling: each day's bidding decisions affect up to $W$ overlapping windows, so setting daily targets requires anticipating future market conditions. We propose SWAG-Bid (Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding), a hierarchical framework decomposing this challenge into episode-level planning and step-level execution. The planner uses a Masked Trajectory Model to forecast markets and generate candidate plans, scored across all overlapping windows by Multi-Window Model Predictive Control Sampling (MWMS) with exponential confidence decay. The controller adjusts reliance on this guidance through a state-adaptive gate, Per-Step Gated Adaptive Layer Normalization (PSG-AdaLN), complemented by Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels carrying budget and constraint information. Experiments on AuctionNet-Sparse and online A/B tests on AliExpress show that SWAG-Bid achieves competitive constraint satisfaction and value acquisition under sliding-window evaluation.

authors: Abhishek A.Sabnis,Mihai Mitrea,Lya Lugon,Karine Sartelet,Marc Bocquet,Xiaoyuan Cheng,Shupeng Zhu,Sibo Cheng
title: From Deterministic to Generative Deep Learning for Urban Air Quality Reconstruction from Sparse Observations
abstract: Full-field reconstruction of air pollution is essential for evaluating pollution exposure and supporting public health decision-making. However, the complex interactions among pollutants, hard-to-predict weather patterns, and limited monitoring station coverage make this a complex task. We apply deep learning techniques to provide fast and accurate reconstructions from sparse observations of four key pollutants: NO2, O3, PM2.5 and PM10. Models are trained on full-field simulation data and evaluated on real-world observations collected from 9 to 28 monitoring stations in the city of Paris. We introduce a diffusion-based generative framework for multi-pollutant reconstruction and benchmark its performance against deterministic deep learning models. Despite noisy observations and strong spatial variability, the models achieve high structural similarity on simulated validation data and produce realistic spatial patterns on real-world observations, as indicated by power-spectrum analysis. We introduce data augmentation methods that enable transfer to real-world observations without retraining, allowing the models to generalise beyond the training period. These findings highlight the potential of ML models for reliable real-world deployment in air pollution reconstruction tasks.

authors: Yuhao Wang,Zelin Zang,Yuxuan Liu,Zhen Lei,Stan Z. Li
title: Graph-structured joint-embedding prediction for single-cell transcriptomics
abstract: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse, unordered measurements of coordinated biological activity, yet many self-supervised models define their learning target at the level of individual genes or reconstructed expression values. Here we introduce GB-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture in which graph-connected gene blocks form the latent prediction units. A student encoder observes the genes outside each target block, whereas an exponential-moving-average teacher represents the full observed gene set. Teacher states are aggregated within a block before the prediction error is evaluated, converting thousands of sparse gene-level targets into a small collection of intermediate-scale latent targets. The graph therefore serves not only as prior information, but also as a mechanism for controlling the structure, scale and predictability of self-supervision. We evaluate the resulting frozen cell representations through objective diagnostics, cell-state annotation, continuous-expression and pathway probes, perturbation-response prediction, computational measurements and direct biological interrogation. This study presents a graph-structured route for adapting JEPA learning to molecular observations and a general framework for designing prediction units from relationships native to a biological modality.

authors: Özkan Canay
title: SoftMCC: An MCC-Brier Calibration Bridge for Threshold-Free Model Selection under Class Imbalance
abstract: Model selection for imbalanced binary classification often uses the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), but its thresholding step makes validation rankings depend on the chosen cutoff. SoftMCC is a post-training MCC validation framework built on established probability-valued confusion counts, coupling an MCC-specific calibrated identity with a tie-aware, shared-pool selection protocol. Its core score is a covariance-normalized probability-label association, reduces exactly to MCC for hard predictions, and is Pearson-bounded. Under perfect population calibration it equals the Brier skill score with identical candidate ordering, which is the calibrated case of Murphy's partition of the Brier score. Outside that regime the gap does not identify calibration error. Across 18 settings with 12 duplicate-safe grouped repeats, SoftMCC attains the best stability mean rank (2.31) and highest mean tie-corrected Kendall's W (0.659), with a significant Friedman test (p=0.004). Nemenyi analysis separates it from area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and MCC@0.5, and 14-source-family sensitivity retains both separations. For selected-model utility, none of six prespecified paired comparisons is significant before or after Holm correction (smallest raw p=0.093), and the dataset-level test is not significant (p=0.746). Label permutation lowers mean W to 0.092. Temperature scaling shifts SoftMCC rankings (mean Spearman 0.851) whereas rank-based and threshold-optimized metrics remain invariant. SoftMCC is a calibration-sensitive MCC-family selector with bounded stability evidence and inconclusive utility differences.

authors: Dipesh Tharu Mahato,Pramod Dhungana
title: ProxyGuard: Direct Reliability Inference for Randomized Data Release Mechanisms with Shared Targets
abstract: Researchers often choose a proxy dataset from many releases, transformations, or seeds. Search can make an invalid release appear adequate, while one adequate release does not establish that its generator is reliable. ProxyGuard controls both errors using prespecified bounded risks and a sealed target set. Named-release mode corrects for multiplicity and certifies specific releases. Direct shared-target mode evaluates independent mechanism draws on a common target, lower-bounds their favorable-score rate, and subtracts a bound on favorable scores contributed by invalid releases. Conditional on the target, release scores are independent, yielding a finite-sample mechanism-reliability guarantee without independent target batches or assumptions on release-level $p$-value dependence. We show that the mean-only penalty is sharp and derive a smooth-score certificate with additive target concentration. In a registered three-requirement study, direct mode raises power from $5.6\%$ to $64.2\%$ at reliability $0.95$, while named mode remains stronger under high-signal evidence. Prospective audits span full-pipeline Rice--TVAE, which retrains on every draw, and a non-tabular text mechanism.

authors: Andrew Gracyk
title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
abstract: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We restrict attention to a descent update rule with natural gradient descent via a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize Calabi-Yau information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via an ill-curvature-conditioned, or lack thereof, landscape. We focus on Calabi-Yau metrics specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential, so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture. In non-compact settings, we can write the metric determinant with respect to a background in terms of a function, pluriharmonic or real. Using Yau's Liouville theorem, we get a partial eigenvalue blow-up effect. In an empirical setting, a Ricci-flat metric will not form, but a blow-up can be a local condition and can hold empirically on open sets even partially in generalized Kähler cases due to lower bounds on the Ricci potential. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist via geometric modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

authors: James Hartley,Zeropy Surio,Daniel Whitmore,Hannah Clarke,Thomas Reed
title: SPARCL: Spectral Partitioned Analytic Continual Learning
abstract: Analytic continual learning has emerged as a strong exemplar-free alternative to gradient-based class-incremental learning because it replaces iterative optimization with closed-form ridge updates. Yet the usual forgetting narrative, centered on stochastic gradient overwriting, does not explain why analytic methods still drift on old classes despite exact recursive solvers. We identify the culprit as spectral interference: the joint ridge classifier for all tasks shares the inverse autocorrelation operator $(R+\lambda I)^{-1}$, so incoming task samples that load onto old dominant eigendirections dilute the spectrum and perturb old-class logits even when old labels are never revisited. Based on this view, we propose SPARCL, a spectral partitioned analytic continual learner that decomposes the running autocorrelation into a high-energy core and a residual complement, freezes old-class classifier components in the core subspace, and updates only the residual block through recursive least squares with an optional residual random-projection expansion. This yields a simple closed-form update with a provable invariance guarantee for the core contribution of old logits. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A under a frozen ViT-B/16 protocol, SPARCL closes most of the gap from classical analytic learners to strong representation matchers, while remaining complementary to sparse feature-decorrelation approaches such as Fly-CL.

authors: Amirhesam Abedsoltan,Enric Boix-Adsera,Fivos Kalogiannis,Mikhail Belkin
title: Revenge of Monosemanticity: Neuron Specialization as a New Form of Feature Learning in MLPs
abstract: Understanding how neural networks learn and organize features is central to understanding their behavior. Much existing theory of feature learning has focused on the emergence of a global low-dimensional representation. We show that this picture is incomplete. In regression problems with clustered data, we demonstrate that multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) develop specialized neurons: individual neurons become strongly aligned with specific features relevant to a particular region of the input space. A substantial fraction of these neurons exhibit monosemanticity: they activate predominantly on inputs from the corresponding cluster. Thus, rather than learning a single global low-dimensional representation, MLPs learn a collection of local low-dimensional representations. Furthermore, we show that this ability to specialize gives MLPs a provable data-efficiency advantage over feature-learning methods based on a global low-dimensional representation.

authors: Sejong Oh
title: Actionable CBFI: Prescriptive Interventional Diagnosis and Interaction-Aware Escalation for Sparse Causal Algorithmic Recourse
abstract: Algorithmic recourse tells an individual which feasible actions would change an unfavourable prediction. Feature attribution explains a prediction, but the most important causes are often not the best levers. We propose Actionable Case-Based Feature Importance (A-CBFI), which turns the descriptive decomposition of Localized-CBFI into a prescriptive, interventional diagnosis on a structural causal model. A-CBFI prescribes the cheapest single action when one exists and searches joint actions only when no single action is enough. We show that interventional interaction also arises from path blocking and shared descendants, which model-only interaction indices cannot see, and that averaged interaction scores cancel where additive targeting fails. On ten tabular benchmarks (6,657 recourse queries), A-CBFI was never significantly less successful than an untargeted causal beam search, prescribed fewer direct actions (1.10 vs 1.38) with fewer model evaluations (119 vs 150), and offered substitutable single actions for 68.2% of the queries a single action solves. Success gains appeared mainly where causes are immutable and single actions are insufficient.

authors: Xiangyu Liu,Zeting Yan,Zhitong Yin,Boyang Li,Xi Zhang
title: MEL: Coordinate-Preserving EEG Tokenization for fMRI Translation
abstract: Background and Objective: Predicting regional blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activity from EEG provides a computational approach to studying electrophysiological-hemodynamic associations. However, changes in input representation, readout architecture, and ensembling can obscure the source of a prediction gain. We investigate the contribution of target-relative spectral estimation under matched readout conditions.Methods: MEL converts each preceding 16-second EEG history into calibrated lag-channel-frequency measurements. Four equal-dimensional representations are compared using matched Ridge and multilayer perceptron (MLP) readouts. The retrospective analysis includes 29 resting-state scans from 22 participants, participant-paired uncertainty estimates, aggregation and correspondence controls, leave-one-participant-out regression, and refitted models on an external Oddball cohort.Results: Morlet-Ridge achieved a mean scan-wise correlation of 0.508 across six regional targets and the global signal, compared with 0.432 for canonical Fourier features. The participant-paired mean difference was 0.069 (95% bootstrap confidence interval, 0.037-0.101), with improvements in 19 of 22 participants. The Morlet MLP prediction ensemble reached 0.491. Shared coordinate permutations preserved prediction after refitting, whereas sample-wise permutations degraded it. Canonical Fourier regression reached 0.377 under participant exclusion; external unseen-participant correlation was 0.026.Conclusions: Spectral estimation materially affected regional BOLD prediction without requiring additional nonlinear readout capacity. MEL provides an explicit measurement interface for controlled comparisons, but weak external results constrain its generalizability. Confirmation requires untouched participant-separated data and split-aware preprocessing.

authors: Oleksandr Cherednichenko,Roman Klypa
title: Suan: Rectifying Direct Preference Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
abstract: Integrating robust safety guardrails into Large Language Models (LLMs) is essential for delivering helpful yet harmless responses. While proprietary systems exhibit reliable safety controls, their underlying methodologies and trade-offs remain largely undisclosed. Achieving comparable security in open-weight models remains a persistent challenge, as post-trained variants frequently suffer from over-refusal and degraded general quality. To overcome these drawbacks, we introduce Suan, a novel preference optimization algorithm. Unlike existing methods, we formulate the optimization objective directly at the gradient level, bypassing the standard variational derivation. As a result, we obtain more interpretable and robust training dynamics. Extensive evaluations across a diverse suite of competitive baselines and benchmarks demonstrate that Suan achieves superior safety alignment while fully preserving response utility.

authors: Lingxiao Qu,Yan Pei
title: Structure and Regularization of Fused Objectives in Kernel Discriminant Analysis for Small-Sample-Size Problems
abstract: When the number of training samples is smaller than the dimension, discriminant analysis faces a singular within-class scatter matrix, and fused objectives that combine the total variance C, the between-class scatter S_b and the within-class scatter S_w are one way to handle it. Using the seven variants of Kernelized Linear Principal Component Discriminant Analysis (KLPCDA) as a platform, we derive the structure of such objectives in this small-sample-size (SSS) setting. The training projections split into a class-mean part and a within-class part, the two scatter operators satisfy WB = 0, and all between-class information lies in the null space of S_w. A single fusion coefficient therefore cannot change the solution, and the variants, KPCA, the regularized kernel Fisher discriminant and the null space methods lie on the boundary of one family with two parameters, the fusion ratio t and a ridge parameter mu. On six tasks from five application domains, the regularized members were more accurate than the best of the seven variants chosen on validation data on all six tasks, by 0.8 to 5.7 points, also under added noise, whereas the fusion ratio gave no gain, including in controlled experiments on dimension ratio, class imbalance and class separation. Selecting a variant per task could gain less than one point, while a fixed choice made on other tasks transferred to every held-out task. The analysis thus gives a principled default for SSS kernel discriminant analysis, with diagnostic quantities, the null space dimension and the class-size spectrum, that can be computed before training.

authors: Zeyu Jia
title: Beyond Embedding Transfer: Component Roles in Grokking Transfer and Stability
abstract: Warm-start transfer accelerates delayed generalization (grokking) on algorithmic tasks, yet which architectural components drive this acceleration and whether transferred circuits remain stable under continued optimization remain unclear. Across a scale-matched 108-run factorial battery ($N=12$ paired seeds), transferring internal attention/MLP matrices ($B$) alongside representations ($E+U$) lifts early accuracy by $5.46$ percentage points and cuts validation confirmation latency by $617$ steps (Holm $p=0.0039$). Whereas readout plus internal blocks ($U+B$) matches full transfer within $\pm 500$ steps in 1-layer models (TOST $p=2.91\times 10^{-13}$), a 2-layer replication confirms internal-block acceleration ($+704.67$ units, $p=4.88\times 10^{-4}$; $8.1\times$ faster trigger) while exposing an inter-block interface where omitting embeddings incurs a $-4{,}475.6$-unit deficit (TOST $p=1.00$). Under continued optimization, unshielded runs suffer severe post-grokking relapse. Freezing carriers ($E+U$) suppresses 1-layer drawdown ($22.06\% \to 0.60\%$ on $2a+b$; $28.56\% \to 5.09\%$ on $3a+b$; $11.09\% \to 0.15\%$ on $a^2+b^2$), but leaves internal blocks vulnerable at high step sizes. Dissecting 12 post-trigger schedules shows that Curvature-Preconditioned Bounded Step-Budget Consolidation ($S_H \approx 0.02, \lambda=1.0$, preserved $v_t$)---via 201-step micro-stepping ($86.6\%$ lower active compute) or exponential decay ($\tau=200$)---compresses drawdown to $0.08\%$--$0.17\%$ on 1-layer $2a+b/3a+b$, $0.13\%$--$0.20\%$ on 2-layer $2a+b$, $0.02\%$ ($66.81\% \to 0.02\%$, Holm $p=0.0020$) on unseen pure-FP32 2-layer subtraction ($a-b$), and $0.09\%$--$0.18\%$ (Holm $p=0.031$) on non-abelian $S_5$ where carrier freezing fails ($10.73\%$ drawdown, $p=0.273$).

authors: Qiulin Shang,Zhoutong Wu,Jie Hu,Kun Yuan
title: QuantForge: Discovering Residual Decompositions for MXFP4 Post-Training Quantization
abstract: Four-bit post-training quantization can reduce the memory demands of large language models, but preserving accuracy under strict MXFP4 W4A4 requires coordinating several design choices. Coordinate transforms change block-encoding errors, which in turn affect the residuals propagated through the network. The useful algorithmic decomposition is therefore not fully known before search. LLM-driven program evolution offers a way to explore these choices, but performance scores alone do not explain which design should change next. We introduce QuantForge, a PTQ discovery system that records competing explanations, selects controls that distinguish them, and checks that successor code implements the resulting conclusions. This residual compilation guides program revisions while retaining useful programs even when their original explanations are rejected. Remeasuring the revised program reveals the next error to address. This process discovers HiRes, a fixed MXFP4 quantizer that shapes coordinates, refines legal code assignments, and recovers errors along attention and MLP paths. Each stage acts on residuals measured after the preceding stage has executed. Across seven tasks, HiRes achieves the lowest seven-model Robust Fit (0.09300) and the lowest quantized Fit-7 at 32B. In matched-budget comparisons of LLM-driven program evolution, each with 240 evaluator calls, QuantForge reaches a held-out transfer target in six of eight runs, compared with three each for textual memory and reflection memory, and one for score-only evolution, despite evaluating fewer new programs. These results show that QuantForge improves the discovery of transferable PTQ algorithms by turning controlled evidence into subsequent program changes. We have open-sourced the QuantForge search framework.

authors: Zeyu Jia
title: Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models: Finite-Division Variety Laws, Semidirect Cascades, and Gradient Saddle Escape
abstract: Structured state-space models (SSMs) achieve linear-time inference and logarithmic-time parallel training via associative scans, yet homogeneous diagonal transitions generate solvable semigroups unable to track non-solvable group words or 3D rigid-body manifolds. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for Non-Commutative Lie-Algebraic State-Space Models (Lie-SSMs), parameterizing recurrent updates on Lie algebra tangent spaces via the matrix exponential. First, via an o-minimal multi-rate cylindrical flag collar, we establish an unconditional single-layer finite-division criterion for homogeneous contracting $SO(3)$ and $SU(2)$ heads, proving odd-prime Sylow abelianity, odd-$p$-core centrality $[u^2,x]=e$, exponent-30 commutator laws ($[u^{30},v^{30}]=e$ in $SO(3)^m$ and $[u^{30},v^{30}]\in Z(G),[u^{30},v^{30}]^2=e$ in $SU(2)^m,SO(4)^m$, excluding $S_5$), and sharp threshold $d^*(S_5)=d^*(A_6)=5$ in $SO(5)$. Second, Depth-2 semidirect and Schreier $2$-cocycle cascades resolve $S_5$, $2I\cong SL_2(F_5)$, and $\mathrm{Heis}(F_p)$ in $O(\log T)$ depth, whereas unnormalized contracting coupling collapses exponentially without Directional RMSNorm. Third, we characterize the $O(\varepsilon^{c-1})$ Chen--Magnus--Hall--Witt commutator saddle and $1/|[G,G]|$ coset-centroid dilution, proving $\varepsilon=0$ symmetry breaking and local Polyak--Łojasiewicz convergence ($\theta_{\max}<\pi$), solving $S_5$ ($99.90\%/99.40\%$ at $T=128$) and $D_{16}$ ($100.00\%$) via dense prefix loss and factored readouts. Across $Q_8,A_5,S_5,D_{16}$, Dyck-2, $SE_2(3)$ Left-Jacobian odometry, GPU scans ($26.03\times$ speedup), and three 3D IMU cohorts (UCI HAR, HAPT-PT 30-subject CV, and REALDISP), Depth-2 Lie-$SO(3)$ cascades reach $95.69\%\pm 0.14\%$ on HAR, $87.16\%\pm 0.64\%$ ($88.32\%\pm 0.93\%$ 30-subject episodes) on HAPT-PT, and $84.23\%\pm 1.00\%$ under displacement on REALDISP.

authors: Michael Vasilakakis(1),Dimitris K. Iakovidis(1) ((1) Department of Computer Science and Biomedical Informatics, University of Thessaly, Lamia, Greece)
title: Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
abstract: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.

authors: Stabak Das,Priyesh Ranjan,Xiangfang Li,Lijun Qian
title: GARV: Graph-Aware Refinement and Safety Verification for High-Level Robot Plans
abstract: High-level robot actions such as goto(region) can hide intermediate traversal, allowing a monitor of the listed actions to accept a plan whose graph-level execution violates a safety rule. We present Graph-Aware Refinement and Verification (GARV), which composes graph-grounded action contracts with a safety monitor to produce a model-relative certificate or counterexample and, when route choice is enforceable, a minimum-cost safe refinement. In a 28-case controlled audit, refinement exposed all 12 targeted hidden hazards and produced the expected verdicts on 16 controls; a separate 14-case SPINE-RoboGuard instantiation yielded two false-safe cases and five action-interface errors. In standalone finite-graph simulation, all 16 designed cases met their expected outcomes, and product verification agreed with exhaustive enumeration on classification, minimum safe hop count, and witness safety in 160 comparisons across 40 graphs. Across 90 graph-contract evaluations on 30 graphs with a hazard deliberately placed on the selected shortest route, GARV found a safe refinement in 72 evaluations and no safe route within the permitted hop bound in 18. For the static forbidden-region rule, synthesis matched a simple hazard-deletion baseline in all 90 evaluations; GARV's guarantees remain conditional on the semantic graph, action contract, safety specification, and enforceability of any selected route.

authors: Kenjiro Ide,Taiga Someya,Kohei Kawaguchi,Keisuke Fujii
title: Strategic Multi-Agent Learning for Interpretable Action Valuation of All Players in Football
abstract: Valuing player actions in football, a complex multi-agent system, requires accounting for strategic interactions among 22 players, including off-ball movements and defensive positioning. Existing reinforcement-learning-based valuation methods commonly incorporate other players through the observed state while retaining independent-agent value formulations. To our knowledge, we introduce the first Markov perfect equilibrium (MPE)-inspired framework for valuing the actions of all 22 players using real football tracking and event data, formulating each possession as a finite-horizon multi-agent dynamic game. To improve interpretability, the framework uses Expandable Decision-Making States (EDMS) and decomposes each Q-value into a successor-feature basis and a linear reward-weight vector. The value basis is estimated through a two-stage procedure combining linear temporal-difference initialization with nonlinear iterative refinement from observed state-action transitions. Using tracking and event data from 95 J1 League matches, we compare the proposed formulation with an independent reinforcement learning baseline under both Position and Velocity States (PVS) and EDMS representations. With EDMS held fixed, the independent baseline assigns the highest value to forward movement in 99.21% of evaluated off-ball states, whereas the most frequent direction under the proposed formulation accounts for 17.63%. Qualitative analyses illustrate context-dependent off-ball valuations and highlight limitations of the current state representation for defensive positioning. Overall, the framework provides an MPE-inspired approach to interpretable action valuation in football, enabling analysis under alternative tactical reward weights.

authors: Elina Rojin Celik,Marcos Medeiros Raimundo,Isabel Valera
title: Learning Pareto Stationary Fronts via Single-Pass Backpropagation
abstract: We propose MOSEL (Multi-Objective Stackelberg Efficient Learning), a framework for a posteriori multi-objective optimization (MOO) in deep neural networks that recovers a full front of Pareto stationary solutions at the computational cost of standard single-objective training. MOSEL reformulates the problem as a bilevel optimization problem that leverages network modularity to decouple representation learning from objective-preference alignment. Casting the bilevel optimization problem as a Stackelberg game enables solving the original a posteriori MOO problem in a single forward-backward pass. As a result, MOSEL matches the time and memory efficiency of standard single-objective training while enabling scalable Pareto stationary front learning. Empirically, MOSEL uncovers diverse and optimal Pareto frontiers in strongly conflicting settings (e.g., fairness-accuracy). Remarkably, even in weakly conflicting regimes such as multi-task learning, it consistently converges to solutions closer to the utopia point, outperforming both standard single-objective training and specialized multi-task learning methods. These results highlight the broader potential of a posteriori MOO learning as a pathway to efficiently learn more diverse and robust representations, ultimately improving generalization.

authors: Avichal Sahai(Ofbusiness),Nishant Raj(Ofbusiness),Animesh Srivastava(Ofbusiness)
title: Lost in the bf16 Cast: Exporting Ternary Language Models Can Revert Most Low-Learning-Rate Code Changes
abstract: Ternary language models such as BitNet b1.58, Falcon-E and BitCPM are fine-tuned through higher-precision latents and deployed as ternary codes by an export that, in the labs' documented pipelines, first casts latents to bf16. We audit releases from three labs. In released checkpoints, fp32 quantization of the shipped latents disagrees with deployed codes on 0.83-1.77% of codes (Falcon-E, BitCPM) and 1.530% (2B-4T); most Falcon-E and BitCPM disagreements are bf16 products exactly on the threshold, which ties-to-even maps to zero, and the unmodified onebitllms exporter reproduces all four Falcon-E releases byte for byte. At fine-tuned endpoints with ULP-matched rates, the documented export lowers greedy GSM8K strict accuracy from 58.79% to 0.78% (Falcon-E-1B-Base) and 36.13% to 0.39% (BitCPM-CANN-0.5B), and a bf16 save and reload lowers 2B-4T's by 27.54 points while its last-number accuracy rises at that endpoint. The strict decrease recurs at each of three new seeds in all three models and has the same direction on 607 reserve test rows, but it is recipe-dependent: at Falcon-E's online-loss-selected rate the export was non-inferior, and after a longer recipe no difference was detected. Two remedies, writing the trained codes directly or adjusting bf16 inputs so unchanged tools emit them, met an inherited 4-point strict-accuracy non-inferiority criterion in all three models, also for the pooled mean over three fixed new trajectories per model and, separately, on the reserve rows. In a frozen study of bf16 latents in fine-tuning (one task, one trajectory per arm), native bf16 writes left 2B-4T's endpoint codes unchanged and changed one Falcon-E code; emulated stochastic-rounding and compensated writers changed codes and were non-inferior to fp32 training at that margin. In two model families, randomized threshold-distance interventions support distance-dependent selection of changed codes.

authors: Zhicheng Cai,Hanlin Wu,Weinan Dai,Yuyan Zhou,Wei-Ying Ma,Ya-Qin Zhang,Hao Zhou
title: Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Yet long-horizon autoregressive rollouts introduce a fundamental limitation: local policy mismatch can compound into severe state distribution shift over trajectories. Existing LLM RL methods, such as GRPO and GSPO, control policy mismatch at the token or sequence level, but overlook this trajectory-induced shift, causing training instability and eventual collapse as the horizon grows. To close the state distribution gap, we propose Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), a principled framework that theoretically derives the state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and incorporates it into the RL objective. TAPO further employs a geometric-mean estimator for variance reduction, together with a length-aware dynamic clipping that prevents overly deviated updates across the trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across eight competition-level benchmarks, achieving up to 48% and 12% improvement over GRPO on mathematical reasoning and algorithmic coding, with substantially enhanced training stability.

authors: Kanghyeon Kim,Johannes F. Lutzeyer,Yanzhu Guo
title: Attention-Graph Curvature for the Verification of Mathematical Reasoning
abstract: Language models have recently solved open Erdős problems and achieved gold-medal level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. But their solutions, written in natural language, cannot yet be verified by proof assistants. An erroneous reasoning step can invalidate every step that comes after, so it is advantageous to detect errors early. Several methods have been proposed to detect erroneous reasoning quickly based on the features of the forward pass of the language model that performs reasoning. In this work, we study whether the directed Forman curvature of that model's attention graph, a local quantity computed at an edge from the attention weights around it, carries information about a step's correctness. To do so, we evaluate four per-step verifiers on ProcessBench with and without the curvature appended to their input. Appending curvature values improves the overall mean performance of all four verifiers. ReProbe, the verifier that takes every token of a step as input, shows the largest improvement. Adding the curvature increases the time of the language model's forward pass by 18% on average. Our code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Gordon V. Cormack,Maura R. Grossman
title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) and Scalable Continuous Active Learning (S-CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.

authors: Yusuf Umut Ciftci,Joonwon Kang,Ajay Suresha Sathya,Somil Bansal
title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website:this https URL

authors: Yuwei Sun,Siyu Zhu
title: MemWM: Associative Memory-Enhanced Latent World Models for Long-Horizon Planning
abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce MemWM, a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. MemWM learns high-level representations directly from observations and uses them to condition predictions via adaptive layer normalization, complementing low-level action-conditioned dynamics within a shared latent space. To prevent memory slots from collapsing into identical representations, we propose two complementary losses that encourage structural diversity across slots and balanced utilization across time steps. On PushT, TwoRoom, Reacher, and OGBCube, MemWM attains an average success rate of 89.9%, matching DINO-WM (89.3%) while using 4$\times$ fewer trainable parameters and no pretrained encoder, and improving over LeWM by 4.1%.

authors: Adibvafa Fallahpour,Parsa Idehpour,Vignesh Kothapalli,Nikita Mounier,Shirley Wu,Shayan Pardis,Jure Leskovec
title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

authors: Yujie Lu,Da Yan
title: What Remains Without Leaking Test Labels? Exposing Evaluation Flaws in Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) identifies unusual graphs in applications such as molecular screening, often using only normal graphs for training. Yet the evaluations of some detectors select models with test labels, and high benchmark scores alone do not show whether detectors recognize structural changes. We audit released code and compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for model states (checkpoints) chosen with and without test labels from the same training run. We separately compare test-tuned hyperparameters with repository defaults and test sensitivity to structural changes while controlling graph size. We evaluate 21 detectors on the UB-GOLD benchmark and on synthetic and molecular graphs with controlled structural changes. About half of the checkpoint-selection gain is linked to choosing a checkpoint and reporting its performance on the same labeled test set. The mean gap persists across training seeds and when normal and anomalous graphs come from different datasets. Most detectors miss many tested structural changes that simple counts detect. With tuned hyperparameters, the two leaders remain the top two by AUROC under every checkpoint rule. Across nine main datasets, test-label checkpoint selection raises the mean AUROC of UB-GOLD's 12 detectors by 5.12 points relative to the final checkpoint.

authors: Xu Zheng,Wei Cheng,Zhuomin Chen,Dongkuan Xu,Mo Sha,Jingchao Ni,Dongsheng Luo
title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. Its runtime fuses the remaining CPU operators and overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, while resumable execution and thermal pacing let training proceed as a background job. We evaluate it on two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms using four LLMs from the Qwen and Llama families. Our workloads cover nightly personalization with labels supplied on the phone and the public LaMP-2 benchmark; comparisons include an optimized CPU trainer, a phone-GPU trainer, forward-only training, and GPU-trained references.

authors: Haoyu Li,Zeren Shui,Yuhao Zhang,Ferhat Erata,Benjamin Mikek,Murali Krishna Ramanathan,Hao Zhou
title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof goals into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.

authors: Bahman Moraffah,Raha Moraffah
title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
abstract: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

authors: Hannan Mahadik,David Salinas,Jacek Golebiowski,Aaron Klein
title: The Shape of the DPO Hyperparameter Landscape: What to Measure, How It Moves with Scale, and When Not to Transfer It
abstract: Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is widely used for language model post-training, but its performance depends strongly on the choice of its hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and the reference-policy regularisation parameter $\beta$. To better understand the DPO hyperparameter landscape, we conduct extensive experiments using a dense hyperparameter grid across different model scales from the same family. This allows us to analyse how the optimal DPO hyperparameters evolve with model size and the number of update steps, with intermediate checkpoints providing an inexpensive signal to accelerate the hyperparameter optimisation process. Furthermore, by evaluating our models on both static and dynamic benchmarks, we identify which benchmarks provide the strongest signal for hyperparameter selection. Finally, we investigate how different state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimisation strategies perform in this setting. Our experiments show that the optimal learning rate varies with model size and that hyperparameters are not transferable across training datasets. We also find that validation loss is a poor proxy for hyperparameter optimisation, as hyperparameters that minimize validation loss only weakly correlate with optimal hyperparameters for downstream benchmarks. Therefore, DPO hyperparameters need to be tuned specifically for the target model, dataset, and evaluation objective. We also show that short candidate training runs can substantially reduce the cost of this selection. We release all our training configurations and evaluation results to support reproducible analysis of selection quality and training cost.

authors: Dwi Sunaryono
title: BRIDGE: An Acceptance Gate to Block False Improvements in Model Updates, with a Retrospective Clinical Evaluation
abstract: Models are updated repeatedly, and an update that looks better on validation data but not on new data is a false improvement that can misguide clinical decisions. The naive rule accepts every positive validation gain and is optimistic when the same data choose and judge the update. BRIDGE is a model-agnostic acceptance gate that decides each update from predictions and the available labels, with fixed settings. Each fold of the data judges the update chosen on the other folds (cross-fitting) to reduce selection bias; acceptance requires the gain's lower bootstrap bound to exceed a margin. The four settings are (A) 11 new datasets, (B) synthetic tasks, (C) 12 retrospective clinical tasks, and (D) 39 supporting datasets. The false-improvement rate falls from 19.1% (naive) to 1.1% (BRIDGE) in (A), 20.7% to 1.7% (B), 20.0% to 0% (C), and 12.5% to 0.5% (D); every 95% confidence interval of the reduction over datasets or tasks excludes zero (not over the clinical sources). An equal-size random draw from the naive acceptances contains more false improvements in (A)-(E) (post hoc, p<0.001). On the OpenML collection (E) of 14 new datasets, the false-improvement rate falls from 25.6% to 1.0%. BRIDGE removes 97% to 100% of the false improvements that the naive rule accepts, and its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times the naive rule's. The 95% upper bound on the false-improvement rate is below 5.5%: formal in (B) for independent tasks (3.56%), and conditional on the real data tested (0.33% to 5.40%).

authors: Adrien Deschenaux,Nadezhda Ilieva,Justin Deschenaux,Manuel Madeira,Dorina Thanou,Aurélien Lucchi,Antonio Orvieto,Caglar Gulcehre,Pascal Frossard
title: Loopholing All the Way: Language Modeling with pure Self-Conditioning
abstract: Recent Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) use Self-Conditioning (SC), or Loopholing, to improve their performance. While SC is traditionally seen as an auxiliary heuristic, its empirical success raises the question: can a continuous generative model be based purely on Self-Conditioning? We answer affirmatively with LAW (``Loopholing All the Way''), which propagates the Expected Embedding under the denoiser's prediction across steps, decoding the tokens once, at the end. On Sudoku, LAW outperforms previous Discrete and Continuous Diffusion Models, including Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. On Maze, LAW is the most accurate from 2 to 64 NFE. After training on TinyGSM and sampling at temperature 1 with 1024 NFE, LAW solves 42.2% of GSM8K problems against 34.5% for uniform Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. Additionally, fine-tuning a pre-trained Uniform Diffusion Model (Duo) with LAW increases its accuracy from 17.2% to 48.1%. Finally, on OpenWebText, LAW pushes the Pareto frontier and approaches Autoregressive Models (ARMs) with 64 NFE. Find our code atthis https URL.

authors: Ismail Huseynov,Stefan Haufe
title: Exact Spectral Uncertainty Decomposition for Linear-Gaussian Bayesian M/EEG Inverse Problems
abstract: Distributed magneto- and electroencephalographic (M/EEG) source reconstruction is a severely underdetermined linear inverse problem. Bayesian source imaging regularizes inversion through source-prior and sensor-noise covariances, but the posterior covariance does not directly distinguish uncertainty constrained by the measurements from uncertainty unobservable under the sensing geometry. We study this distinction for linear-Gaussian M/EEG models with diagonal source-prior and sensor-noise covariances, covering Type-I inference and Type-II inference conditional on learned covariance hyperparameters. After restricting the analysis to the prior-supported source space, standardizing the prior, and whitening the sensor noise, the complete singular spectrum of the forward operator separates likelihood-visible and likelihood-null directions. This yields an additive uncertainty decomposition of the conditional posterior covariance: uncertainty in likelihood-visible directions is reduced according to spectral information content, whereas likelihood-null uncertainty remains unchanged from the prior. The spectral representation also yields a prior-minus-reduction identity, showing that covariance reduction is confined to the likelihood-visible subspace. Spectral markers quantify likelihood information and prior-variance retention and reduction. Fixed-orientation MEG simulations with adaptive noise learning illustrate the framework. Dense Bayesian minimum-norm inference retains a large likelihood-null component, whereas sparse $\gamma$-MAP strongly reduces the fitted prior support. Within that support, the markers distinguish strongly informed directions from a weakly constrained direction. Thus, prior-support selection determines which source coordinates remain in the fitted model, while the spectral decomposition quantifies how strongly the retained directions are constrained by the measurements.

authors: Matheus Calheira Guimarães de Oliveira,Marco Aurélio da Silva Cruz,Regis Cardoso,Lucas Cambuim,Rafael Macieira,Arthur Paim,Helaine Neves,Alex Santos,Lilian Guarieiro,Jean Schmith,Prashant Kumar,Erick G. Sperandio Nascimento
title: Benchmarking Model Compression Techniques Across Heterogeneous Edge Platforms: A Predictive Maintenance Use Case for Rotating Machinery
abstract: To enable Industry 5.0, where autonomous systems are widely adopted and integrated with people to promote sustainable development in industries, it is imperative to adapt complex deep learning models to operate efficiently on resource-constrained hardware for edge inference. However, adapting these models remains challenging due to the hardware heterogeneity of edge computing in industrial settings, performance degradation caused by model compression, and the lack of clear guidance on which compression techniques are practical and effective for applications such as predictive maintenance. To address these challenges, this paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four state-of-the-art model compression techniques applied to a high-performance convolutional neural network for predictive maintenance using a real-world dataset of rotating machinery, equipment typically used in industry. The compressed models were evaluated across a heterogeneous set of nine computing platforms, ranging from highly constrained edge computing devices to general purpose and high-performance processors, reflecting the diversity and fragmentation typical of industrial edge environments. By jointly prioritizing classification performance, inference speed, and compression ratio, we found that compression using knowledge distillation emerged as the most effective approach. The model had more than 90% speedup across all devices while maintaining a 91.22% balanced F-score, with a very small drop in predictive performance relative to the uncompressed model, along with a 98.9% size reduction. Through successful deployment across multiple edge platforms and a systematic comparison of compression strategies, we demonstrated a clear path to achieving Industry 5.0 targets, drastically cutting computational costs and, consequently, energy consumption without sacrificing predictive performance.

authors: Zeropy Surio,Tobias Engel,Mei-Lin Chou,Anika Raman,Samuel Okafor
title: Same Luck, Different Choice: Twin-World Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning rewards a complete episode, yet the policy needs credit for every decision inside it. Counterfactual branching estimates this credit by re-running the episode after an alternative decision, but the branch draws its sampling noise independently of the factual episode, so the outcome difference mixes the effect of the decision with the luck of everything that follows. We observe that in agentic search the retriever, the corpus, and the grader are deterministic, so an episode is a deterministic function of the policy's decisions and its sampling noise. Twin worlds are therefore realizable: the same noise, a different decision. We introduce TWICE (TWIn-world Credit Estimation), which keys the Gumbel noise of every token by turn and line, rolls out counterfactual twins that inherit the factual episode's downstream noise, and turns their paired outcome differences into turn-level advantages for policy-gradient updates on actor-sampled trajectories; only the actor is deployed. Twin credit is unbiased for any coupling quality, its variance is that of an independent counterfactual scaled by $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the twins' outcome correlation, and under coupling the number of rollouts needed to resolve an advantage of size $\Delta$ falls from $\Theta(\Delta^{-2})$ to $\Theta(\Delta^{-1})$. A square-root rule spends the twin budget where outcomes are predicted to disagree per unit cost. On seven question-answering benchmarks, TWICE improves the average exact match of GRPO by 5.3 and 4.5 points on Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, outperforms tree-search and counterfactual-branching baselines, and uses 68% fewer auxiliary tokens than VinePPO.

authors: Jonathan T. Barron,Dan Gnanapragasam,Michael Tschannen
title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
abstract: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously observed "slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $\epsilon$ hyperparameter.

authors: Sangeeta Warrier,Anush Sankaran,Ryen W. White
title: CuraLoc: Repository-Level Fault Localization via Planned Code Inspection
abstract: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. Existing repository-level localization methods often let language models iteratively decide what code to inspect next, requiring repeated model calls and substantial token usage. We investigate whether these inspection decisions can instead be planned before source retrieval. In this research, we introduce CuraLoc, which first selects candidate files and represents their symbols using compact behavioral and structural descriptions. In a single planning decision, the model jointly selects starting symbols, chooses code relationships to inspect from each, and forms hypotheses about likely edits. Deterministic retrieval collects the requested source for a final ranking informed by those hypotheses, concentrating model reasoning on choosing and comparing code rather than directing each retrieval step. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on the SWE-Bench Lite and Verified datasets. On SWE Bench Verified with GPT-5.2, CuraLoc raises Func@1 from LocAgent's 53.8% to 59.3% while using 90.3% fewer recorded tokens, and also outperforms RepoSearcher (56.2%) and Agentless (39.6%) on Func@1. On SWE-bench Lite, CuraLoc achieves a high 83.8% Func@5 accuracy improving on Agentless by more than 15% in relative accuracy. Additionally, CuraLoc supports different model backbones, with strong localization accuracy demonstrated using both GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra. These results provide evidence that repository-level code inspection can be planned effectively without iterative model-controlled navigation.

authors: Sean Bin Yang,Zongyi Xu,Jilin Hu,Ying Sun,Kristian Torp,Bin Yang,Torben Bach Pedersen,Christian S. Jensen
title: Rethinking Multi-View Fusion for Urban Representation Learning
abstract: Urban region representation learning encodes heterogeneous urban signals, such as mobility flows, points of interest, and land-use patterns, into unified embeddings for downstream tasks, including check-in prediction, crime forecasting, and service demand estimation. Existing approaches rely on globally shared fusion and joint optimization, implicitly assuming uniform modality importance and naturally balanced multi-objective training. However, urban data is inherently heterogeneous. Our empirical analysis reveals two structural issues: (i) modality utility varies markedly across regions, causing static fusion to overemphasize signals from certain modalities; and (ii) heterogeneous objectives exhibit persistent gradient imbalance, causing representational bias and unstable training. We present PRISM, a self-adjusting framework for adaptive multi-view learning. PRISM adapts sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing to learn region-specific view allocations, while a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID)-inspired regulation mechanism mitigates gradient conflicts during optimization. Experiments on three large-scale urban datasets show that PRISM achieves more competitive performance than strong multi-view baselines, while providing more stable optimization behavior and more balanced region representations.

authors: Tareque Mohmud Chowdhury,Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal
title: Tree Depth and Sample-Quality-Associated Features: Two Hidden Factors in Boruta Selection for RNA-Seq Data Classification
abstract: Boruta is a widely used method for selecting gene panels from RNA sequencing data, and its most used implementation recommends Random Forest trees of depth 3 to 7, an untested setting. We tested whether this setting changes which genes are selected, using pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (10,469 tumors, 33 cancer types) and breast cancer PAM50 subtyping (981 tumors, 5 subtypes). A leakage-free protocol fitted every label-dependent step inside training folds, measured every effect against seed-to-seed variation, and held out a locked test set per task. In pan-cancer data, shallow trees changed the selection far more than a new seed did: the top-500 overlap with unlimited-depth selections was 0.37 at depth 5, against 0.84 to 0.93 between seeds at depth 5 or unlimited depth. Shallow trees confirmed 3.5 times fewer genes, missed markers of large classes and produced less accurate 50-gene panels (balanced accuracy 0.809 vs 0.889). The effect vanished once the cap reached about 60 to 75% of the depth that unrestricted trees grow to, set mainly by the number of classes, not sample size, and leaving depth uncapped cost no accuracy in either task. The effect replicated in a second cross-validation repeat and under permutation importance. About a third of pre-filtered candidates also tracked sample quality within class; a within-class filter removed them without loss of test accuracy (balanced accuracy 0.943 vs 0.942 with 1,000 genes). We recommend uncapped trees, or a cap chosen from the realized tree depth, and a within-class quality filter before Boruta.

authors: Yuxing Peng,Zhiqing Tang,Weijia Jia
title: The Cost of an Unknown Horizon for the Last Iterate of Clipped SGD under Heavy-Tailed Noise
abstract: Training is often stopped at a data-dependent time, so guarantees for the last iterate must hold at all times simultaneously. We determine the optimal time-uniform rate for the last iterate of clipped SGD on smooth convex objectives under heavy-tailed noise with a bounded central $p$th moment, $1<p\le2$. A schedule without horizon or confidence inputs attains $\tilde O(t^{-\beta_p})$ at all times, with $\beta_p=2(p-1)/(3p-1)$, also almost surely, and no rule that steps along the stochastic gradient at its current iterate attains $\tilde O(t^{-r})$ for any $r>\beta_p$, even with adaptive step sizes and thresholds. This rate lies between the optimal rate $O(T^{-\alpha_p})$ for a known horizon $T$, $\alpha_p=(p-1)/p$, and the previous time-uniform rate $\tilde O(t^{-2(p-1)/(3p)})$ (Chezhegov et al., ICLR 2026); under finite variance, the exponents are $1/2$, $2/5$, and $1/3$. Their conjecture that a better schedule reaches the optimal rate thus holds with a known horizon (Liu; Jiang et al.) but fails without one. Querying gradients at the running average attains $\tilde O(t^{-\alpha_p})$ at all times, whereas heavy-ball momentum with geometric forgetting and polynomially bounded steps cannot improve on $\beta_p$.

authors: Zhi-Song Liu,Helmi Toropainen,Ammar Kheder,Michael Boy
title: Climate downscaling with likelihood functional flow matching
abstract: Decisions about heat, frost and flooding are made locally, yet reanalyses and climate models resolve tens of kilometres. Generative downscalers add kilometre-scale detail with uncertainty, but are tied to a grid, costly to sample and lack a tractable likelihood. Here we introduce CD-FFM, a functional flow-matching model that treats the high-resolution field as a continuous random field that one model can query at any location and resolution. Its velocity acts pointwise, so spatial variability comes from a noise prior fitted to the observed spectrum and every observation has an exact likelihood. Downscaling ERA5 to 1 km daily temperature over Fennoscandia, CD-FFM lowers the continuous ranked probability score by 27-31% against regression and 12-18% against a forty-times larger neural operator in each of three test years, and outperforms a CorrDiff-style diffusion model while sampling about fifty times faster. The same model transfers to precipitation and makes large kilometre-scale ensembles affordable.

authors: Yuxuan Xia,Wenbo Lu,Shaoyi Zheng,Shengjie Wang
title: INTRA: Interleaved Non-contiguous Token spaRse Attention
abstract: Transformers achieve strong performance across modalities but are bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of attention. Sparse attention can reduce this cost, but effective sparsity must preserve useful long-range communication and map well to GPU hardware. We introduce INTRA--Interleaved Non-contiguous Token spaRse Attention--a hardware-aware static sparse attention design based on a relay-communication view under Computational Query Set (CQS) constraints. Rather than directly covering all token-to-token interactions within each sparse layer, INTRA uses complementary sparse groups to provide short mediated communication paths across layers. Scatter forms relay groups that sample broadly across local neighborhoods, while Gather reconnects these groups in subsequent layers. Under a partition model, this structure guides CQS-compatible sparse patterns with global reachability. Our CQS-aware FlashAttention-style kernel computes structured indices at runtime, loads selected non-contiguous tokens, and packs them densely for computation. On an A100, INTRA achieves a $1.53\times$ speedup in $2K$ FLUX.1-dev generation, with better measured image quality than evaluated CLEAR configurations after LoRA self-distillation. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, it improves long-context prefill efficiency with strong teacher-forced retrieval performance under matched LoRA adaptation. Attention-only benchmarks further show up to $8.4\times$ and $10.4\times$ speedups over MoBA and density-constrained NSA, respectively. Code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Cheng Gui,Xiang Zheng,Yutao Wu,Hanxun Huang,Yige Li,Kaidi Xu,Cong Wang,Wei-Ying Ma
title: SEEK: Skill Extraction with Evolving Knowledge against Frontier Science Agents
abstract: Science agents increasingly package domain expertise as reusable skills that plan analyses, select tools, and execute workflows. This modularity creates a confidentiality risk: the interactions that deliver a skill's capability can also reveal the skill itself. We build an extensible benchmark of 40 protected skills across eight open- and closed-source science-agent platforms, comparing direct, fixed-strategy, and bandit-guided iterative probing under reference-based and reference-free evaluation. Leakage is pervasive: all eight platforms (100%) leak at least one protected skill, and four reach 100% attack success under a single direct request. To stress-test platforms that resist simple probing, we propose SEEK (Skill Extraction with Evolving Knowledge), a black-box, self-evolving red-teaming agent that consolidates response-derived evidence in persistent memory and evolves reusable attack skills, using only user-visible responses. On 12 skills from SpatialAgent and Biomni, SEEK achieves 100% attack success while reducing the mean first-success round by 31.8% and 38.2% relative to bandit-guided probing. Against a confidentiality policy that blocks all three benchmark protocols, SEEK still extracts one of six protected skills. These findings show that current science agents do not reliably protect their skills and that defenses must be evaluated against adaptive, multi-turn attackers.

authors: Hanne Raum,Jasper Hoffmann,Joschka Boedecker
title: STeP-TS: Shared Temporal Filters with Pruning for Time Series
abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting requires capturing temporal dependencies across multiple scales while accounting for both shared and variable-specific dynamics. Compact forecasting models have emerged as an attractive alternative to increasingly large architectures, but preserving strong predictive performance within tight computational and memory budgets remains challenging. We propose a compact one-layer convolutional framework that learns a shared bank of multi-scale temporal filters of each variable. Lightweight variable-specific scalar weights determine the contribution of each temporal component, enabling the model to capture shared temporal structure while adapting to variable-specific dynamics. The learned weights and filter-output energy further provide a natural signal for structured pruning of convolutional filters, reducing computational complexity with minimal degradation in forecasting performance. We additionally introduce an amplitude-adaptive normalization mechanism that preserves variable-dependent temporal amplitudes. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate forecasting performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially fewer parameters and inference FLOPs and achieving low per-sample latency.

authors: Yilong Li,Chengpo Yan,Yijing Zeng,Hanlei Wu,Mingjun Song,Suman Banerjee
title: Shared Context, Separate Engines: Streaming Vision--Language Inference on Edge SoCs
abstract: Edge SoCs pack CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, yet vision--language model (VLM) runtimes keep generation on one engine and leave the others idle. Streaming VLMs expose further parallelism: new frames arrive while earlier queries are still being answered. Engines differ in compute and memory access and contend when they co-run, so no single placement of stages wins across SoCs and workloads. Backend-local KV state keeps other engines from continuing the work. \name coordinates heterogeneous accelerators to execute stateful VLM inference concurrently. It separates a stream's versioned context from each engine's KV state, so any engine can continue the stream by reusing, importing, or reconstructing that state.
